passages.t: David's sons in Hebron and Jerusalem
passages.happening: ‘These were the sons of David who were born to him in Hebron’ (verse 1): Amnon, Daniel, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah and Ithream, each with his mother's name (verses 1-3). David reigned in Hebron ‘seven years and six months’ and in Jerusalem ‘thirty-three years’ (verse 4). In Jerusalem four sons were born to him ‘by Bathsheba daughter of Ammiel’ (verse 5), with Solomon last, and nine more sons by other wives (verses 6-8). The list ends, ‘And Tamar was their sister’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 2 traced Judah down to David. Now comes David's own family, the spine of the book's hope.

Royal households were large, and kings married for alliance as well as love. Absalom's mother, Maacah, was the daughter of the king of Geshur, a small kingdom north-east of the Sea of Galilee. A king's mother mattered to the succession, so the list names each son's mother.

In the Hebrew of verse 5 Bathsheba's name is spelled Bath-shua, and her father is Ammiel; in 2 Samuel she is the daughter of Eliam, and the two forms of his name use the same parts in reverse order. Solomon is named last of her four sons, a reminder that he was not the obvious heir. His name comes from the root of shalom, peace.

Readers who know 2 Samuel will hear the names: Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah all died in struggles over the family and the throne, and Tamar's story is one of the saddest in Scripture. The list tells none of it, and does not need to.
passages.later: Second Samuel gives the same years: ‘In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah’ (2 Samuel 5:5).
passages.asks: A list of names hides a family's griefs. Ask whose story you know only as a name. And ask what it means that God's promise ran through a household as troubled as David's.

passages.t: The kings, the captive, and the line after the exile
passages.happening: From Solomon the list runs king by king, each ‘his son’, to Josiah (verses 10-14). Josiah's sons follow, then Jehoiakim's son Jeconiah (verses 15-16). Then: ‘The descendants of Jeconiah the captive’ (verse 17): Shealtiel his son, Pedaiah and others (verse 18). ‘The sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei’ (verse 19). Zerubbabel's children and grandchildren follow for several generations (verses 19-24).
passages.hearers:
In a few verses the chapter passes over four centuries, every king on David's throne from Solomon to the last kings before the fall of Jerusalem. The list names only David's sons who reigned, so it passes over Queen Athaliah, who seized the throne for six years and was not of David's line. Near the end the steady chain of his son breaks, as brothers and an uncle succeed one another in Judah's last years.

Where Kings ends with the exile, this list keeps going. Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, was taken to Babylon in 597 BC. Clay tablets found in Babylon, listing rations for royal dependents, name Jehoiachin king of Judah and his sons, a rare outside witness to the exiled family. Jeconiah is called the captive, but his line does not end in Babylon. It runs through Zerubbabel, who governed Judah around 520 BC and led the rebuilding of the temple, and on to men of the Chronicler's own time.

For readers without a king, this was quiet and powerful evidence: David's house still existed, and God's promise to David had not been cancelled by the exile. Names in the later generations carry the hope of the families who gave them; Hasadiah means the LORD is kind.
passages.later: Jeremiah said of Jeconiah, ‘None of his descendants will prosper to sit on the throne of David’ (Jeremiah 22:30). Haggai later told Zerubbabel, ‘I will make you like My signet ring, for I have chosen you’ (Haggai 2:23). Matthew runs Jesus' line through ‘Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the exile to Babylon’ (Matthew 1:11), and Luke through David's son ‘Nathan’ (Luke 3:31).
passages.hard:
Who was Zerubbabel's father, Pedaiah or Shealtiel?

Verse 19 names Zerubbabel as a son of Pedaiah, while Ezra, Haggai and Matthew call him the son of Shealtiel. Pedaiah and Shealtiel were brothers, both sons of Jeconiah. Readers have offered a few explanations. One is a levirate marriage: if Shealtiel died without a son, his brother Pedaiah may have married the widow, and the child counted legally as Shealtiel's, as the law describes. Another is that Pedaiah was the natural father and Zerubbabel was raised as Shealtiel's heir, perhaps as next in the royal line. Some also note that the Greek translation of Chronicles reads Shealtiel here. Whatever the answer, all the sources agree that Zerubbabel was Jeconiah's grandson and belonged to the house of David.
passages.asks: The list keeps going after the captive king, through generations of waiting. Ask what promise you are still waiting on, and how you keep it in view. And ask what you are naming, in your children or your work, after the hope you hold.
